name: uring-sync
workload: Local recursive directory copy on NVMe, cold cache: 100K x 4KB files and 100K x 100KB files; also network transfer vs rsync over SSH.
claimed_speedup: cp -r 7.67s vs 5.14s (1.5x) for 100K x 4KB; 22.7s vs 5.4s (4.2x) for 100K x 100KB; network 9.7GB/100K files 165s vs rsync 390s (58% faster)
tradeoffs: Linux only, kernel 5.7+ for splice, needs liburing, fmt, OpenSSL; kTLS network mode uses pre-shared secret protocol, not SSH.
caveats: No CPU model, disk type, kernel version, compiler flags or cp version stated; benchmark script in tests/perf but hardware missing; small repo (10 commits); 60MB/10K-file network case is about equal to rsync.
found_via: WebSearch: github io_uring file copier C++ faster than cp (Show HN: File copier 4x faster than cp using io_uring)

name: wcp
workload: Copy 20 x 512MiB, 7000 x 1MiB and 200000 x 1KiB files on a Samsung NVMe SSD with 64GB RAM using io_uring.
tradeoffs: Linux only (kernel 5.6+), experimental, not robust enough for daily use per author; standalone tool, not a library.
caveats: Numbers from README only; CPU model, SSD model, cp version and compiler flags not stated; cache state unspecified; last commit 2021.

name: al-dente (dent)
baseline: GNU find (readdir/fts directory traversal); also fd
workload: Listing a synthetic tree of 765,200 entries with a multithreaded getdents64 walker, timed with hyperfine (3 warmups, 10 runs).
claimed_speedup: find 3.178s vs dent 563.9ms (5.64x faster); fdfind 1.633s (dent 2.90x faster)
tradeoffs: Linux only (getdents64); lists names only, no stat; README says AI-assisted derivation of a coworker's code.
caveats: No hardware or compiler flags; single synthetic scenario (benchmark_scenario.c generates it); license unclear (README says provided as-is; no confirmed LICENSE file, a repo page summary said MIT); fd run uses -HI but system time exceeds wall time so comparison involves threads in both; warm cache implied.
found_via: WebSearch: github C fast recursive directory scan getdents64 benchmark faster than find

name: LLFIO
baseline: POSIX read/write (physical device latency used as reference)
workload: Software overhead of 4Kb reads/writes on NVMe and SATA flash compared with device latency; zero-copy file i/o design with mmap and io_uring backends.
claimed_speedup: Claims i/o overhead around 100 nanoseconds on Linux; README gives NVMe Linux <30 microseconds at 99th percentile (numbers from README summary, no direct baseline ratio)
tradeoffs: Large API surface (P1031 proposal); standardisation attempt abandoned in 2025; needs C++17.
caveats: No head-to-head against read/write or mmap on the page I opened; claim is overhead vs device latency, not a speedup over a named baseline; hardware and flags not stated there. Benchmark detail may live in docs not opened.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ asynchronous file IO library benchmark faster than std::filesystem

name: file_io_benchmark (Windows unbuffered multi-threaded loading)
workload: Loading 1,000 chunks of 1 MiB (1.0 GB) from NVMe on Windows with unbuffered multi-threaded reads versus fread and memory mapping, 5 repetitions.
claimed_speedup: Unbuffered auto threads 11.3-11.4 GB/s vs fread 4.2-5.0 GB/s (auto) and memory mapping 6.8-7.3 GB/s (auto); single-thread memory mapping 1.2 GB/s
tradeoffs: Windows APIs; benchmark code and technique, not a reusable library.
caveats: No license; compiler and flags not stated; 1 GB cached-or-not state unspecified; 2 commits; fread baseline uses C stdio, not mmap/io_uring on Linux. Technique harvested from benchmark shootout.
